Boundedness and stabilization in a two-species chemotaxis-competition system of parabolic-parabolic-elliptic type

Masaaki Mizukami 00 0 E-mail: masaaki.mizukami.math@gmail.com

Department of Mathematics, Tokyo University of Science

1-3, Kagurazaka, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 162-8601, Japan

August 24, 2026

  • Abstract. This paper deals with the two-species chemotaxis-competition system

    {ut=d1Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w)+μ1u(1−u−a1v)in​Ω×(0,∞),vt=d2Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w)+μ2v(1−a2u−v)in​Ω×(0,∞),0=d3​Δ​w+α​u+β​v−γ​win​Ω×(0,∞),\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v)&{\rm in}\ \Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w)+\mu_{2}v(1-a_{2}u-v)&{\rm in}\ \Omega\times(0,\infty),\\ 0=d_{3}\Delta w+\alpha u+\beta v-\gamma w&{\rm in}\ \Omega\times(0,\infty),\end{cases}

    where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, n≥2n\geq 2; χi\chi_{i} and μi\mu_{i} are constants satisfying some conditions. The above system was studied in the cases that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2}, and it was proved that global existence and asymptotic stability hold when χiμi\frac{\chi_{i}}{\mu_{i}} are small ([5, 32, 34]). However, the conditions in the above two cases strongly depend on a1,a2a_{1},a_{2}, and have not been obtained in the case that a1,a2≥1a_{1},a_{2}\geq 1. Moreover, convergence rates in the cases that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2} have not been studied. The purpose of this work is to construct conditions which derive global existence of classical bounded solutions for all a1,a2>0a_{1},a_{2}>0 which covers the case that a1,a2≥1a_{1},a_{2}\geq 1, and lead to convergence rates for solutions of the above system in the cases that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and a1≥1>a2a_{1}\geq 1>a_{2}.

1 Introduction

Many phenomena, which appear in natural science, especially, biology, chemistry and physics, support animals’ lives. In this paper we focus on chemotaxis which is one of the important properties and is related to e.g., movement of sperm, migration of neurons or lymphocytes and tumor invasion. Chemotaxis is the property such that species move towards higher concentration of the chemical substance when they plunge into hunger.

A mathematical problem which describes a part of the life cycle of cellular slime molds with chemotaxis is called the Keller–Segel system:

ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v),τvt=Δv+u−v,u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\quad\tau v_{t}=\Delta v+u-v,

where χ>0\chi>0 and τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. Moreover, the chemotaxis system with growth terms

ut=Δu+χ∇⋅(u∇v)+κu−μu2,τvt=Δv+u−vu_{t}=\Delta u+\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\kappa u-\mu u^{2},\quad\tau v_{t}=\Delta v+u-v

was proposed by [25, 31], where χ,κ,μ>0\chi,\kappa,\mu>0 and τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}. After the pioneering work of Keller–Segel [19], the Keller–Segel system and the chemotaxis system are intensively studied (see e.g., [2, 13, 15]). A generalized problem of Keller–Segel systems, which means a two-species chemotaxis system, was proposed in [36] and also has studied (see e.g., [3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 21, 37]; global existence was proved in [7, 8, 37]; and thier asymptotic stability was shown in [37]; related works which deal with blow-up of solutions can be seen in [3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 21]). Recently, a two-species chemotaxis system with competitive kinetics

ut=Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w)+μ1u(1−u−a1v),\displaystyle u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),
vt=Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w)+μ2v(1−a2u−v),\displaystyle v_{t}=\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w)+\mu_{2}v(1-a_{2}u-v),
τ​wt=Δ​w+α​u+β​v−γ​w\displaystyle\tau w_{t}=\Delta w+\alpha u+\beta v-\gamma w

with some χ1,χ2,μ1,μ2,a1,a2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2},\mu_{1},\mu_{2},a_{1},a_{2}>0 and τ∈{0,1}\tau\in\{0,1\}, which describes the evolution of two competing species which react on a single chemoattractant, was proposed by Tello–Winkler [34] and was studied (see [1, 22, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 38]). About this problem with τ=1\tau=1, global existence and boundedness was obtained in the 2-dimensional case ([1]) and the nn-dimensional setting ([22]); moreover, asymptotic behavior of solutions was established in [1, 27]. Related works which dealt with global existence and boundedness in this two-species problem with sensitivity functions can be found in [27, 38]; and related works which treated the non-competition case are in [26, 28, 29, 30]. These results in the case τ=1\tau=1 are motivated by the results ([5, 32, 34]) in the case τ=0\tau=0. Therefore the parabolic-parabolic-elliptic problem reduced by letting τ=0\tau=0 seems to be helpful to analyze the fully parabolic case.

In this paper we consider the two-species chemotaxis system with competitive kinetics of parabolic-parabolic-elliptic type

{ut=d1Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w)+μ1u(1−u−a1v),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=d2Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w)+μ2v(1−a2u−v),x∈Ω,t>0,0=d3​Δ​w+α​u+β​v−γ​w,x∈Ω,t>0,∇u⋅ν=∇v⋅ν=∇w⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\[2.84526pt] v_{t}=d_{2}\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w)+\mu_{2}v(1-a_{2}u-v),&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\[2.84526pt] 0=d_{3}\Delta w+\alpha u+\beta v-\gamma w,&x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\[2.84526pt] \nabla u\cdot\nu=\nabla v\cdot\nu=\nabla w\cdot\nu=0,&x\in\partial\Omega,\ t>0,\\[2.84526pt] u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\;v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),&x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (1.1)

where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2n\geq 2) with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega and ν\nu is the outward normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The constants d1,d2,d3,χ1,χ2,μ1,μ2,a1,a2d_{1},d_{2},d_{3},\chi_{1},\chi_{2},\mu_{1},\mu_{2},a_{1},a_{2} and α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma are positive. The initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} are assumed to be nonnegative functions. The unknown functions u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) represent the population densities of two species and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) shows the concentration of the chemical substance at place xx and time tt.

The problem (1.1) is a problem on account of the influence of chemotaxis, diffusion, and the Lotka–Volterra competitive kinetics, i.e., with coupling coefficients a1,a2>0a_{1},a_{2}>0 in

ut=u⁡(1−u−a1​v),vt=v⁡(1−a2​u−v).\displaystyle u_{t}=u(1-u-a_{1}v),\quad v_{t}=v(1-a_{2}u-v). (1.2)

The mathematical difficulties of the problem (1.1) are to deal with the chemotaxis term ∇⋅(u∇w)\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w) and the competition term u⁡(1−u−a1​v)u(1-u-a_{1}v). To overcome these difficulties, in the case that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and d3=α=β=1d_{3}=\alpha=\beta=1 in (1.1), Tello–Winkler [34] applied comparison methods to this problem and obtained global existence of classical bounded solutions and their asymptotic behavior under the conditions that

2​(χ1+χ2)+a2​μ1<μ2and2​(χ1+χ2)+a1​μ2<μ1.\displaystyle 2(\chi_{1}+\chi_{2})+a_{2}\mu_{1}<\mu_{2}\quad\mbox{and}\quad 2(\chi_{1}+\chi_{2})+a_{1}\mu_{2}<\mu_{1}. (1.3)

However, if χ1→0\chi_{1}\to 0 or μ1→∞\mu_{1}\to\infty, then these conditions break down. Recently, it was shown that the conditions

χ1μ1∈[0,d32​α)∩[0,a1​d3β),χ2μ2∈[0,d32​β)∩[0,a2​d3α),\displaystyle\frac{\chi_{1}}{\mu_{1}}\in\left[0,\frac{d_{3}}{2\alpha}\right)\cap\left[0,\frac{a_{1}d_{3}}{\beta}\right),\quad\frac{\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}}\in\left[0,\frac{d_{3}}{2\beta}\right)\cap\left[0,\frac{a_{2}d_{3}}{\alpha}\right), (1.4)
a1​a2​d32<(d3−2​α​χ1μ1)​(d3−2​β​χ2μ2)\displaystyle a_{1}a_{2}d_{3}^{2}<\left(d_{3}-\frac{2\alpha\chi_{1}}{\mu_{1}}\right)\left(d_{3}-\frac{2\beta\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}}\right) (1.5)

lead to global existence and asymptotic stability in (1.1) in the case that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) ([5]). The conditions (1.4)–(1.5) partially relax (1.3) in view of the point mentioned above. On the other hand, in the case that a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2} and d3=β=1d_{3}=\beta=1 in (1.1) Stinner–Tello–Winkler [32] established global existence and stabilization of global classical solutions when

χ1μ1≤a1,χ2μ2<12and\displaystyle\frac{\chi_{1}}{\mu_{1}}\leq a_{1},\quad\frac{\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}}<\frac{1}{2}\quad\mbox{and}
α​χ1μ1+max⁡{χ2μ2,a2​(μ2−χ2)μ2−2​χ2,(α−a2)​χ2μ2−2​χ2}<1\displaystyle\frac{\alpha\chi_{1}}{\mu_{1}}+\max\left\{\frac{\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}},\frac{a_{2}(\mu_{2}-\chi_{2})}{\mu_{2}-2\chi_{2}},\frac{(\alpha-a_{2})\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}-2\chi_{2}}\right\}<1

are satisfied. In summary the two-species chemotaxis-competition model (1.1) were studied in the cases that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2}, and it was proved that global existence and same asymptotic behavior as solutions to the Lotka–Volterra competition model (1.2) hold when χiμi\frac{\chi_{i}}{\mu_{i}} are small. However, the conditions in the above two cases strongly depend on a1,a2a_{1},a_{2}, and have not been obtained in the case that a1,a2≥1a_{1},a_{2}\geq 1. Moreover, convergence rates in the cases that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2} have not been studied.

The purpose of this work is to construct conditions which derive global existence of classical bounded solutions for all a1,a2>0a_{1},a_{2}>0 which covers the case that a1,a2≥1a_{1},a_{2}\geq 1, and lead to convergence rates for solutions of (1.1) in the cases that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) and a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2}.

For establishing global existence and boundedness we shall suppose that χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} and μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2} satisfy the following conditions:

χ1μ1<n​d3n−2​min​{1α,a1β}andχ2μ2<n​d3n−2​min​{1β,a2α}.\displaystyle\frac{\chi_{1}}{\mu_{1}}<\frac{nd_{3}}{n-2}\min\left\{\frac{1}{\alpha},\frac{a_{1}}{\beta}\right\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\frac{\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}}<\frac{nd_{3}}{n-2}\min\left\{\frac{1}{\beta},\frac{a_{2}}{\alpha}\right\}. (1.6)

We assume that the initial data u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} satisfy

0≤u0∈C⁡(Ω¯)∖{0},0≤v0∈C⁡(Ω¯)∖{0}.\displaystyle 0\leq u_{0}\in C(\overline{\Omega})\setminus\{0\},\quad 0\leq v_{0}\in C(\overline{\Omega})\setminus\{0\}. (1.7)

Now the main results read as follows. The first one is concerned with global existence and boundedness in (1.1).

Theorem 1.1.

Let d1,d2,d3>0d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}>0, μ1,μ2>0\mu_{1},\mu_{2}>0, a1,a2>0a_{1},a_{2}>0, χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, α,β,γ>0\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0 and let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2)(n\geq 2) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Assume that (1.6) are satisfied. Then for any u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} satisfying (1.7) with some q>nq>n, there exists an exactly one pair (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of nonnegative functions

u,v∈C⁡(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞)),\displaystyle u,\;v\in C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty)),
w∈C⁡(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞))∩Lloc∞​([0,∞),W1,q​(Ω)),\displaystyle w\in C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty))\cap L^{\infty}_{\rm loc}([0,\infty);W^{1,q}(\Omega)),

which satisfy (1.1). Moreover, the solutions u,v,wu,v,w are uniformly bounded, i.e., there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,q​(Ω)≤Cfor all​t≥0,\displaystyle\|{u(\cdot,t)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|{v(\cdot,t)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|{w(\cdot,t)}\|_{W^{1,q}(\Omega)}\leq C\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\geq 0,

and the solutions u,v,wu,v,w are the Hölder continuous functions, i.e., there exist θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and M>0M>0 such that

‖u‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖v‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖w‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])≤Mfor all​t≥1.\displaystyle\|u\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\|v\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\|w\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}\leq M\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\geq 1.
Remark 1.1.

This result give the existence of global classical bounded solutions in the case that a1,a2≥1a_{1},a_{2}\geq 1. Moreover, the condition (1.6) relaxes (1.4) which assumed for global existence of solutions in [5]. Indeed, if χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} and μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2} satisfy the condition (1.4), then χ1,χ2\chi_{1},\chi_{2} and μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2} satisfy the condition (1.6). However, the condition (1.6) does not always relax those assumed in [32] and [34]; in the case that a1,a2∈(0,1)a_{1},a_{2}\in(0,1) the condition (1.6) relaxes (1.3) under the condition

χ1<2​n​a1​(χ1+χ2)​(1+a1)(n−2)​(1−a1​a2)andχ2<2​n​a2​(χ1+χ2)​(1+a2)(n−2)​(1−a1​a2),\displaystyle\chi_{1}<\frac{2na_{1}(\chi_{1}+\chi_{2})(1+a_{1})}{(n-2)(1-a_{1}a_{2})}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\chi_{2}<\frac{2na_{2}(\chi_{1}+\chi_{2})(1+a_{2})}{(n-2)(1-a_{1}a_{2})},

and in the case that a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2} the condition (1.6) relaxes the condition

α​χ1μ1+χ2μ2<1,\displaystyle\frac{\alpha\chi_{1}}{\mu_{1}}+\frac{\chi_{2}}{\mu_{2}}<1,

which was used to obtain global existence in [32], when

α⁡(n−2)n<min⁡{1,a1​α,a2}\frac{\alpha(n-2)}{n}<\min\{1,a_{1}\alpha,a_{2}\}

hold.

The main theorem tells us the following result in the 2-dimensional case.

and

μ1>χ12​(1+δ1)​(1−a1)​(α2​a1​δ1+β2​a2−α​β​a1​a2​(1+δ1))4​a1​d1​d3​γ​(1−a1​a2)​(4​δ1−a1​a2​(1+δ1)2),\displaystyle\mu_{1}>\frac{\chi_{1}^{2}(1+\delta_{1})(1-a_{1})(\alpha^{2}a_{1}\delta_{1}+\beta^{2}a_{2}-\alpha\beta a_{1}a_{2}(1+\delta_{1}))}{4a_{1}d_{1}d_{3}\gamma(1-a_{1}a_{2})(4\delta_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}(1+\delta_{1})^{2})}, (1.9)

Remark 1.2.

Theorem 1.4.

Let d1,d2,d3>0d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}>0, μ1,μ2>0\mu_{1},\mu_{2}>0, a1≥1a_{1}\geq 1, a2∈(0,1)a_{2}\in(0,1), χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, α,β,γ>0\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0 and let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2)(n\geq 2) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Assume that there exists a unique global classical solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of (1.1) such that

‖u‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖v‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖w‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])≤Mfor all​t>0\displaystyle\|u\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\|v\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\|w\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}\leq M\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>0

with some M>0M>0. Then under the conditions (1.11)–(1.12), (u,v,w)(u,v,w) has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    If a1>1a_{1}>1 and take a1′∈(1,a1]a^{\prime}_{1}\in(1,a_{1}] in (1.11)–(1.12), then there exist C>0C>0 and ℓ>0\ell>0 satisfying

    ‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(t)−1‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(t)−βγ‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​e−ℓ​tfor all​t>0.\displaystyle\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(t)-1\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\left\|w(t)-\frac{\beta}{\gamma}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\ell t}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>0.
  2. (ii)

    If a1=1a_{1}=1, then there exist C>0C>0 and ℓ>0\ell>0 satisfying

    ‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(t)−1‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(t)−βγ‖L∞​(Ω)≤C​(t+1)−ℓfor all​t>0.\displaystyle\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(t)-1\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\left\|w(t)-\frac{\beta}{\gamma}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C(t+1)^{-\ell}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>0.
Remark 1.3.

If the assumption of Theorem 1.1 and (1.11)–(1.12) are satisfied, then Theorem 1.4 gives the convergence rates for solutions in the cases that a1>1>a2a_{1}>1>a_{2} and a1=1>a2a_{1}=1>a_{2}. Moreover, the conditions (1.11)–(1.12) are the same conditions as that assumed in [27] in the case that a1≥1>a2a_{1}\geq 1>a_{2} and h⁡(u,v,w)=α​u+β​v−γ​wh(u,v,w)=\alpha u+\beta v-\gamma w.

Remark 1.4.

Stabilization in the case that a1,a2≥1a_{1},a_{2}\geq 1 is a still open question. In the case that a1,a2>1a_{1},a_{2}>1 a Lotka–Volterra competition model with diffusion term was studied; however, its analysis is difficult and it is known that solutions have complicated structures (see cf. [9, 16, 17, 18, 20, 23, 24]).

The strategy of the proof of Theorem 1.1 is to extend a method in [33] to a two-species case. We first aim to establish the LpL^{p}-estimate for uu with some p>n2p>\frac{n}{2} from the following derivative of ∫Ωup\int_{\Omega}u^{p}:

1pdd​t∫Ωup≤(p−1)χ1∫Ωup−1∇u⋅∇v+μ1∫Ωup(1−u−a1v).\displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\leq(p-1)\chi_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p-1}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\mu_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}(1-u-a_{1}v). (1.13)

Since the third equation in (1.1) derives that

(p−1)χ1∫Ωup−1∇u⋅∇v\displaystyle(p-1)\chi_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p-1}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v =(p−1)​χ1d3​p​∫Ωup​(α​u+β​v−γ​w),\displaystyle=\frac{(p-1)\chi_{1}}{d_{3}p}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}(\alpha u+\beta v-\gamma w), (1.14)

we shall show that a combination of (1.13) and (1.14), along with the condition (1.6) implies

dd​t​∫Ωup≤−c1​(∫Ωup)p+1p+c2​∫Ωup,\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\leq-c_{1}\left(\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\right)^{\frac{p+1}{p}}+c_{2}\int_{\Omega}u^{p},

which leads to LpL^{p}-estimate for uu. Then aided by standard semigroup estimates, we can obtain the L∞L^{\infty}-estimate for uu. On the other hand, one of the keys for the proof of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 is to derive the following energy estimate:

dd​tE(t)≤−ε∫Ω[(u(⋅,t)−u¯)2+(v(⋅,t)−v¯)2+(w(⋅,t)−w¯)2]\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}E(t)\leq-\varepsilon\int_{\Omega}\left[(u(\cdot,t)-\overline{u})^{2}+(v(\cdot,t)-\overline{v})^{2}+(w(\cdot,t)-\overline{w})^{2}\right] (1.15)

for all t>0t>0 with some positive function EE and some constant ε>0\varepsilon>0, where (u¯,v¯,w¯)∈ℝ3(\overline{u},\overline{v},\overline{w})\in\mathbb{R}^{3} is a solution of (1.1). Thanks to (1.15), we can obtain that there exists C>0C>0 such that

∫0∞∫Ω(u−u¯)2+∫0∞∫Ω(v−v¯)2+∫0∞∫Ω(w−w¯)2≤C,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(u-\overline{u})^{2}+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(v-\overline{v})^{2}+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(w-\overline{w})^{2}\leq C,

which together with the regularity of the solution leads to Theorems 1.3 and 1.4.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we prove global existence and boundedness (Theorem 1.1) through a series of lemmas. Section 3 is devoted to the proof of asymptotic stability (Theorems 1.3 and 1.4); we first provide some lemmas which will be used later, and we next devide the section into Sections 3.1 and 3.2 according to the proof of Theorem 1.3 and that of Theorem 1.4, respectivly.

2 Global existence and boundedness

In this section we shall show global existence and boundedness in (1.1). First we will recall the known result about local existence of solutions to (1.1) ([5, Lemma 2.1], [32, Lemma 2.1]).

Lemma 2.1.

Let d1,d2,d3>0d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}>0, μ1,μ2>0\mu_{1},\mu_{2}>0, a1,a2>0a_{1},a_{2}>0, χ1,χ2>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2}>0, α,β,γ>0\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0 and let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n∈ℕ)(n\in\mathbb{N}) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Then for any u0,v0u_{0},v_{0} satisfying (1.7) for some q>nq>n, there exist Tmax∈T_{\rm max}\in (0,∞](0,\infty] and an exactly one pair (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of nonnegative functions

u,v,w∈C⁡(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))\displaystyle u,\;v,\;w\in C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\rm max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\rm max}))

which satisfy (1.1). Moreover,

e​i​t​h​e​r​Tmax=∞o​rlimt→Tmax(‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω))=∞.\displaystyle either\ T_{\rm max}=\infty\quad or\quad\lim_{t\to T_{\rm max}}(\|{u(\cdot,t)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|{v(\cdot,t)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})=\infty.

We next give the LpL^{p}-estimate for uu with some p>n2p>\frac{n}{2} which plays an important role in deriving L∞L^{\infty}-estimate for uu. The proof is based on the proof of [33, Lemma 2.2].

Lemma 2.2.

Assume that (1.6)–(1.7) are satisfied. Then for all p∈I1p\in I_{1}, there exists C⁡(p)>0C(p)>0 such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖Lp​(Ω)≤C⁡(p)\displaystyle\|{u(\cdot,t)}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\leq C(p)

for all t>0t>0, where

I1:=(n2,min⁡{α​χ1(α​χ1−d3​μ1)+,β​χ1(β​χ1−a1​d3​μ1)+}).I_{1}:=\left(\frac{n}{2},\min\left\{\frac{\alpha\chi_{1}}{(\alpha\chi_{1}-d_{3}\mu_{1})_{+}},\frac{\beta\chi_{1}}{(\beta\chi_{1}-a_{1}d_{3}\mu_{1})_{+}}\right\}\right).

We fix p∈I1p\in I_{1}. Here we note from the condition (1.6) that I1≠∅I_{1}\neq\emptyset. Multiplying the first equation in (1.1) by up−1u^{p-1} and integrating it over Ω\Omega, we obtain that

=(p−1)χ1∫Ωup−1∇u⋅∇v+μ1∫Ωup(1−u−a1v).\displaystyle=(p-1)\chi_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p-1}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\mu_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}(1-u-a_{1}v). (2.1)

Then integration by parts and the third equation in (1.1) imply that

=(p−1)​χ1d3​p​∫Ωup​(α​u+β​v−γ​w).\displaystyle=\frac{(p-1)\chi_{1}}{d_{3}p}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}(\alpha u+\beta v-\gamma w). (2.2)

Therefore a combination of (2.1) with (2.2) yields that

1p​dd​t​∫Ωup≤μ1​∫Ωup−(μ1−α⁡(p−1)​χ1d3​p)​∫Ωup+1−(a1​μ1−β⁡(p−1)​χ1d3​p)​∫Ωup​v.\displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\leq\mu_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}-\left(\mu_{1}-\frac{\alpha(p-1)\chi_{1}}{d_{3}p}\right)\int_{\Omega}u^{p+1}-\left(a_{1}\mu_{1}-\frac{\beta(p-1)\chi_{1}}{d_{3}p}\right)\int_{\Omega}u^{p}v.

Recalling p∈I1=(n2,min⁡{α​χ1(α​χ1−d3​μ1)+,β​χ1(β​χ1−a1​d3​μ1)+})p\in I_{1}=\left(\frac{n}{2},\min\left\{\frac{\alpha\chi_{1}}{(\alpha\chi_{1}-d_{3}\mu_{1})_{+}},\frac{\beta\chi_{1}}{(\beta\chi_{1}-a_{1}d_{3}\mu_{1})_{+}}\right\}\right) that

we establish from the Hölder inequality

that there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 satisfying

1p​dd​t​∫Ωup≤−ε​(∫Ωup)p+1p+μ1​∫Ωup,\displaystyle\frac{1}{p}\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\leq-\varepsilon\left(\int_{\Omega}u^{p}\right)^{\frac{p+1}{p}}+\mu_{1}\int_{\Omega}u^{p},

Similarly, we can confirm the following LpL^{p}-estimate for vv with some p>n2p>\frac{n}{2}.

Now we could construct all estimates which will enable us to obtain the estimate for the solution; Lemmas 2.2 and 2.3 lead to the following lemma. Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Lemma 2.4 directly shows Theorem 1.1. ∎

3 Stabilization

In this section we will establish stabilization of solutions to (1.1). Here we assume that there exists a unique global classical solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of (1.1) satisfying

‖u‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖v‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])+‖w‖Cθ,θ2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])≤Mfor all​t≥1\displaystyle\|u\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\|v\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}+\|w\|_{C^{\theta,\frac{\theta}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}\leq M\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\geq 1

with some M>0M>0. we first recall a important lemma for the proof of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 (see [14, Lemma 4.6]).

Lemma 3.1.

Let n∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,∞))n\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty)) satisfy that there exist constants C∗>0C^{*}>0 and θ∗>0\theta^{*}>0 such that

‖n‖Cθ∗,θ∗2​(Ω¯×[t,t+1])≤C∗for all​t≥1.\displaystyle\|n\|_{C^{\theta^{*},\frac{\theta^{*}}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+1])}\leq C^{*}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\geq 1.

Assume that

∫0∞∫Ω(n⁡(x,t)−N∗)2​𝑑x​𝑑t<∞\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}(n(x,t)-N^{\ast})^{2}\,dxdt<\infty

with some constant N∗>0N^{\ast}>0. Then

We next provide the following lemma which will be used to confirm that the assumption of Lemma 3.1 is satisfied.

Lemma 3.2.

Let a,b,c,d,e,f∈ℝa,b,c,d,e,f\in\mathbb{R}. Suppose that

a>0,d−b24​a>0,f−c24​a−(2​a​e−b​c)24​a​(4​a​d−b2)>0.\displaystyle a>0,\quad d-\frac{b^{2}}{4a}>0,\quad f-\frac{c^{2}}{4a}-\frac{(2ae-bc)^{2}}{4a(4ad-b^{2})}>0.

Then

a​x2+b​x​y+c​x​z+d​y2+e​y​z+f​z2≥0\displaystyle ax^{2}+bxy+cxz+dy^{2}+eyz+fz^{2}\geq 0

holds for all x,y,z∈ℝx,y,z\in\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

Straightforward calculations lead to the conclusion of this lemma (for more details, see [27, Lemma 3.2]). ∎

Finally, we give the following lemma which enables us to upgrade the L2L^{2}-convergence rate to L∞L^{\infty}-convergence rate.

Lemma 3.3.

Let (u¯,v¯,w¯)∈ℝ3(\overline{u},\overline{v},\overline{w})\in\mathbb{R}^{3} be a solution to (1.1). Assume that there exists a decreasing function h:[0,∞)→ℝh:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} satisfying

holds for all f∈L∞​(Ω)f\in L^{\infty}(\Omega), which means from the boundedness of u,vu,v that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u¯‖Lp​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)−v¯‖Lp​(Ω)≤C1​(p)​h​(t)2pfor all​t>0\displaystyle\|{u(\cdot,t)-\overline{u}}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}+\|{v(\cdot,t)-\overline{v}}\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\leq C_{1}(p)h(t)^{\frac{2}{p}}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>0

with some C1​(p)>0C_{1}(p)>0. Here (2.5) enables us to see that

‖w⁡(⋅,t)−w¯‖W2,2​n+2​(Ω)≤CE​(2​n+2)​C1​(2​n+2)​h​(t)1n+1for all​t>0.\displaystyle\|w(\cdot,t)-\overline{w}\|_{W^{2,2n+2}(\Omega)}\leq C_{E}(2n+2)C_{1}(2n+2)h(t)^{\frac{1}{n+1}}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>0.

Thus we have that there is C2>0C_{2}>0 such that

Then by using a similar argument as in the proof of [1, Lemma 3.6] we infer that there exists C3>0C_{3}>0 such that

≤C3​C4​h​(t−1)1n+1for all​t>1,\displaystyle\leq C_{3}C_{4}h(t-1)^{\frac{1}{n+1}}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>1,

Lemma 3.5.

Assume that (1.8)–(1.10) are satisfied. Then

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u∗‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)−v∗‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)−w∗‖L∞​(Ω)→0as​t→∞.\displaystyle\|{u(\cdot,t)-u^{\ast}}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|{v(\cdot,t)-v^{\ast}}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|{w(\cdot,t)-w^{\ast}}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0\quad\mbox{as}\ t\to\infty.

A combination of Lemmas 3.1 and 3.4 implies this lemma. ∎

Next we desire to establish convergence rates for the solution of (1.1). We note that in view of Lemma 3.3 it is sufficient to confirm the L2L^{2}-convergence rates for the solution.

Lemma 3.6.

Assume that (1.8)–(1.10) are satisfied. Then there exist C>0C>0 and ℓ>0\ell>0 such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u∗‖L2​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)−v∗‖L2​(Ω)≤C​e−ℓ​tfor all​t>0.\displaystyle\|{u(\cdot,t)-u^{\ast}}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}+\|{v(\cdot,t)-v^{\ast}}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\leq Ce^{-\ell t}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>0.

Aided by Lemma 3.5 and the L’Hôpital theorem, a similar argument as in the proof of [1, Lemma 3.7] (or [27, Proof of Theorem 1.2]) derives that there exist C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 and t0>0t_{0}>0 such that for all t>t0t>t_{0},

C1​(∫Ω(u−u∗)2+∫Ω(v−v∗)2)≤E1≤C2​(∫Ω(u−u∗)2+∫Ω(v−v∗)2),\displaystyle C_{1}\left(\int_{\Omega}(u-u^{\ast})^{2}+\int_{\Omega}(v-v^{\ast})^{2}\right)\leq E_{1}\leq C_{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}(u-u^{\ast})^{2}+\int_{\Omega}(v-v^{\ast})^{2}\right), (3.6)

dd​t​E1​(t)≤−C3​E1​(t)for all​t>t0\displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}E_{1}(t)\leq-C_{3}E_{1}(t)\quad\mbox{for all}\ t>t_{0}

with some C3>0C_{3}>0, which implies that there exists C4>0C_{4}>0 such that

Thus a combination of (3.6) and (3.7) yields that

∫Ω(u−u∗)2+∫Ω(v−v∗)2≤C4C1​e−C3​t,\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}(u-u^{\ast})^{2}+\int_{\Omega}(v-v^{\ast})^{2}\leq\frac{C_{4}}{C_{1}}e^{-C_{3}t},

which concludes the proof of this lemma. ∎

In this subsection we will obtain stabilization in the case that a1≥1>a2a_{1}\geq 1>a_{2}. In this case we also have to confirm that the assumption of Lemma 3.1 is satisfied.

Lemma 3.7.

Assume that (1.11)–(1.12) are satisfied. Then there exist a nonnegative function E2:(0,∞)→ℝE_{2}:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} and constants ε1≥0\varepsilon_{1}\geq 0 and ε2>0\varepsilon_{2}>0 such that

holds for all t>0t>0. Moreover, there exists C>0C>0 satisfying

Proof of Theorems 1.3 and 1.4.
